analysis.one_liner: Forces companies to divest their pharmacies if they also own a drug middleman or insurer.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would break up the largest drug-pricing and pharmacy conglomerates, has sat untouched in the House Judiciary Committee since it was introduced with support from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for one company to own a pharmacy and also own a health insurer or a pharmacy benefit manager — the middlemen that decide which drugs are covered, what patients pay, and what pharmacies get reimbursed. Companies like the ones behind the biggest drug plans would have one year to sell off their pharmacy businesses. Enforcement would come from the FTC, the Justice Department's antitrust division, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits with triple damages for people who were overcharged.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay for prescriptions, independent and community pharmacies that compete against insurer-owned drugstores, and taxpayers, since the bill's findings argue insurers hide profits in unregulated pharmacy units to get around limits on insurance profits. People overcharged at vertically integrated pharmacies could recover triple damages from a fund built out of disgorged revenue.

how_it_helps.text: It ends the common ownership of pharmacies and the companies that steer prescriptions to them, which the FTC has found reduces competition and raises drug costs for patients.

It orders any company that owns a pharmacy plus an insurer or PBM to divest the pharmacy within one year, with 10 percent of monthly profits held in escrow until it complies and a trustee empowered to sell the pharmacy if it does not.

It gives HHS's Inspector General, the FTC, the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and individual patients the power to sue violators, with treble damages, attorney's fees, and disgorgement of pharmacy revenue into a fund for overcharged consumers.
It requires FTC and Justice Department review of every divestiture and lets both agencies block future deals that would re-create the same conflicts of interest.

analysis.who_pays: The large health care conglomerates that own drugstores alongside insurance and PBM businesses would have to sell those pharmacies, giving up a highly profitable part of their operations. Some of the transition cost could reach consumers in the short run if networks are disrupted during the one-year divestment window.

drawbacks.text: The one-year deadline to divest is aggressive; a botched or rushed sale of a large pharmacy business could disrupt prescription access for some patients during the transition.

Defenders of vertical integration argue that insurer-owned pharmacies can lower costs through scale and that steering to affiliated pharmacies is not always harmful; the bill's findings take the opposite view, and Congress is effectively settling that dispute by mandate rather than by case-by-case antitrust review.

The bill reaches hospital pharmacies, long-term care pharmacies, and mail-order operations alike, so divestment could force sales of parts of integrated provider systems that patients experience as convenient one-stop care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — separating the referee of drug pricing from the pharmacies it pays — addresses a conflict of interest documented by the FTC and cited in the bill's own findings, including more than 7,000 pharmacy closures between 2019 and 2024. The main honest cost is transition risk: unwinding companies this large in twelve months is hard, and enforcement depends on agencies doing their jobs. On balance the design is aggressive but direct, with escrow penalties and a trustee fallback to prevent companies from simply waiting out the deadline.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-May 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where no hearing, markup, or vote has been taken since.

narrative.text: Representative Diana Harshbarger introduced the bill in the House on May 13, 2026, joined by original cosponsors from both parties.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no further steps since.

The bill's findings state that the six largest PBMs are each part of large health care conglomerates that processed more than 90 percent of U.S. prescriptions in 2023, and that the FTC has found these integrated PBMs steer business to their own pharmacies at patients' expense.
The bill's findings also cite the closure of more than 7,000 pharmacies between 2019 and 2024, which it links to PBMs pressuring independent pharmacies into unfavorable contracts.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the large insurer-PBM-pharmacy conglomerates the bill targets are better off: the bill sits in committee with no scheduled action, and the status quo — insurers owning the pharmacies their own drug plans steer patients toward — continues. Patients and independent pharmacies remain waiting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The big drug-pricing conglomerates, for now

for.name: Rep. Diana Harshbarger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote it to force structural separation of PBMs, insurers, and pharmacies.

for.name: Original cosponsors (Reps. Auchincloss, Carter of Georgia, Landsman, Nehls, Nadler)
for.what_they_did: Signed on at introduction from both parties, giving the bill a bipartisan core of support.

for.name: 8 cosponsors total (5 Democrats, 3 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Added bipartisan backing to the bill after introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support is evenly split across party lines: its sponsor is a Republican, and its eight cosponsors break down as 5 Democrats and 3 Republicans.

industries.industry: Insurer-PBM-pharmacy conglomerates (CVS Health, UnitedHealth/OptumRx, Cigna/Express Scripts)
industries.note: The bill would force these companies to sell their pharmacy businesses within a year, unwinding the vertical integration by which the three biggest PBMs steer prescriptions to drugstores they own. Their profit from that arrangement comes directly out of what patients and health plans pay for drugs, which is why their interest runs against the public's here.

The bill's findings say PBM market power contributed to more than 7,000 pharmacy closures between 2019 and 2024; removing insurer-owned competitors and the steering that favors them restores these pharmacies' customer base. When local pharmacies close, patients lose convenient access to prescriptions.

Insurers would have to divest pharmacy holdings, and the bill targets their practice of shifting profits into unregulated pharmacy units to evade Medical Loss Ratio limits — a constraint meant to make insurers spend premium dollars on care rather than overhead and profit.

analysis.trajectory: With more than half the session's remaining time gone, no committee action on the record, and no sign of a Judiciary markup, the bill's most realistic paths are a standalone committee vote if the chair schedules one, or a provision folded into a larger health or antitrust package. Most bills at this stage — introduced and referred but never marked up — die when the Congress ends in January 2027.
